title: Blood Spot in an Egg: What It Is and Whether It Is Safe to Eat

seo.title: Blood Spot in an Egg: Is It Safe to Eat?
seo.meta_description: A small blood spot in an egg usually comes from a tiny ruptured blood vessel during ovulation and does not mean the egg is fertilized or unsafe. USDA says it can be eaten if the egg was properly stored and has no other spoilage signs.
seo.search_intent: Understand why blood spots occur in eggs, whether they mean fertilization, whether the egg is safe, and which signs actually require discarding it.

excerpt: A small blood spot on the yolk or in the white usually forms when a tiny blood vessel ruptures during ovulation or egg formation. USDA states that this does not make the egg unsafe. It also does not mean the egg is fertilized. If the shell was intact, storage was appropriate, the odor is normal, and the white has no unusual pink or iridescent discoloration, the egg can be cooked normally.
content_html:
A small blood spot inside an egg does not mean the egg is spoiled and does not, by itself, make it unsafe. USDA explains that these spots form when one or more tiny blood vessels rupture around the time of ovulation.

The spot may look red, brown, or dark reddish and can occur on the yolk or in the white. It is mainly a quality appearance issue rather than automatic evidence of contamination.

The spot forms before the shell is completed

A yolk is released from the ovary and travels through the oviduct, where albumen, membranes, and finally the shell are added.

If a tiny vessel breaks during that process, a very small amount of blood can become enclosed inside the finished egg.

As pigments oxidize, an older blood spot may appear brown rather than bright red without necessarily indicating spoilage.

A blood spot does not mean the egg was fertilized

The common idea that a blood spot is an embryo is incorrect. Fertilization and a minor vascular rupture are separate biological events.

Commercial eggs can contain blood spots even when hens have never had contact with a rooster.

The material comes from the hen's reproductive tissues, not from a developing chick.

Why do some eggs have them more often?

Frequency can vary with hen age, genetics, stress, and normal reproductive physiology. Young hens beginning to lay and selected older hens may show more irregularities in ovulation.

Commercial candling catches many visible defects by shining light through eggs, but very small spots can still pass through grading.

Finding an occasional blood spot in a retail carton is therefore not unusual.

USDA says blood spots are not a special safety risk

USDA's shell-egg guidance explicitly states that blood spots result from ruptured small vessels and do not indicate that the egg is unsafe.

If the appearance bothers you, the spot can be removed with the tip of a clean spoon or knife before cooking.

Removing it is cosmetic rather than a required safety step.

Do not confuse a spot with abnormal egg-white color

USDA distinguishes a localized blood spot from pink, greenish, or iridescent albumen. Pink or iridescent egg white can be associated with bacterial spoilage and is a reason to discard the egg.

A clearly unpleasant odor after cracking is also a discard sign.

A tiny localized red speck is fundamentally different from widespread discoloration of the white.

Shell condition and storage still matter

The blood spot does not cancel normal egg-safety rules. Use eggs with intact shells, keep them refrigerated where required, and avoid extended room-temperature storage.

A cracked shell makes it easier for microorganisms on the exterior to enter the egg.

Evaluate the blood spot and the shell condition as separate issues.

Does it need extra cooking?

No special cooking is required because of the spot. Cook the egg according to the same safety guidance as any other shell egg.

FDA and USDA recommend firm whites and yolks for maximum safety, particularly for higher-risk people, or appropriately pasteurized eggs for undercooked recipes.

The blood spot itself does not make Salmonella more likely.

What should you do when you find one?

Crack the egg into a separate small bowl, check the smell and overall appearance, and remove the spot only if you prefer.

If everything else is normal and the egg was handled properly, it can be used.

The practical rule: a small blood spot is a minor ovulation-related irregularity, not evidence of fertilization or spoilage.

faq.question: Can you eat an egg with a blood spot?
faq.answer: Yes. USDA says a small blood spot does not mean the egg is unsafe.

faq.question: Does a blood spot mean there is an embryo?
faq.answer: No. It comes from a small ruptured blood vessel in the hen and does not prove fertilization.

faq.question: When should an egg be discarded?
faq.answer: Discard eggs with bad odor, abnormal pink or iridescent whites, compromised shells with poor handling history, or other clear spoilage signs.
